draft.title: Angles at a point and on a line
card: On a line
Angles on a straight line add to \(180^{\circ}\). If one angle is \(50^{\circ}\), the angle beside it on the line is \(180^{\circ} - 50^{\circ} = 130^{\circ}\).
At a point

Angles around a point add to \(360^{\circ}\), a full turn. If three angles at a point are \(100^{\circ}\), \(120^{\circ}\) and \(90^{\circ}\), the fourth is \(360^{\circ} - 310^{\circ} = 50^{\circ}\).
Vertically opposite
When two straight lines cross, the angles facing each other across the crossing point are equal. They are called vertically opposite angles.
The two lines make four angles. Each angle and its neighbour lie on a straight line, so they add to \(180^{\circ}\).
draft.remember: Line: 180. Point: 360. Vertically opposite angles are equal.

a.q: Two angles lie on a straight line. One is \(65^{\circ}\). What is the other?
a.why: Angles on a straight line add to \(180^{\circ}\), so the other is \(180^{\circ} - 65^{\circ} = 115^{\circ}\). Using \(360^{\circ}\) gives \(295^{\circ}\), but that rule is for angles at a point, not on a line.
a.clue: A straight line is half a full turn.

b.q: Four angles meet at a point: \(90^{\circ}\), \(110^{\circ}\), \(x\) and \(2x\). What is the value of \(x\)?
b.why: Angles at a point add to \(360^{\circ}\), so \(3x = 360^{\circ} - 200^{\circ} = 160^{\circ}\). Then \(x\) is \(160^{\circ} \div 3\), about \(53^{\circ}\). The value \(160^{\circ}\) is \(3x\), not \(x\).
b.clue: Add the known angles first, then share what is left.

wants.brief: Two straight lines crossing at a point, making four angles. One pair of vertically opposite angles is marked with matching arcs, and the other pair with double arcs.
wants.why: It shows which angles face each other across the crossing point.

problems.detail: The exact answer is \(x = 160^{\circ} \div 3 = 53\tfrac{1}{3}^{\circ}\), so the option \(53^{\circ}\) is not 'the value of x'. The question never asks students to round, yet the why says 'about \(53^{\circ}\)'. Change the known angles so x is a whole number (for example \(90^{\circ}\) and \(120^{\circ}\) give \(3x = 150^{\circ}\), \(x = 50^{\circ}\)), or ask for x to the nearest degree.

The question needs students to combine \(x + 2x = 3x\) and solve \(3x = 160^{\circ}\), but the card only shows subtracting known angles. Algebra is not taught here, and the clue 'share what is left' is vague about splitting in the ratio 1:2.

check.summary: Question a is correct. In question b the exact answer is \(53\tfrac{1}{3}^{\circ}\), so the option \(53^{\circ}\) is only approximate and the question never asks for rounding. Use angles that give a whole-number x. The question also relies on algebra the card does not teach.

b.q: Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles is \(40^{\circ}\). What is the size of the angle beside it?
